author: Aarush

WavLate: Audio Retrieval goes Multi-Vector

Community Article Published
November 20, 2026 Upvote 3 Aarush chungimungi

TL;DR. WavLate is, to our knowledge, the first open late-interaction model trained for searching audio with text and text with audio. It keeps one vector for every 0.31 seconds of sound and one vector for every word of a caption, and lets each word find its best-matching moment in the clip. One general model, with no fine-tuning per dataset, reaches a mean Recall@1 of 37.9 across AudioCaps and Clotho. That is the best result among the nine open audio and text models we evaluated on the same test pools. The weights, the training data with its mined hard negatives, and the test pools are all released. The same recipe built on the M2D-CLAP audio encoder (WavLate-M2D) reaches 41.9, which is 5.5 points above M2D-CLAP itself.

📚 Training data: chungimungi/WavLate-training-data

Introduction

Audio and text retrieval covers two tasks. In text to audio retrieval, a person types a description such as "a dog barks while cars pass" and the system returns the matching recordings from a sound library. In audio to text retrieval, the system receives a recording and returns the captions that describe it. Sound designers searching effect libraries, archivists indexing field recordings and researchers filtering large audio collections all depend on this kind of search.
Almost every open model for this job follows the CLAP recipe (Contrastive Language and Audio Pretraining) [1, 2]. CLAP trains two encoders, one for audio and one for text, so that a clip and its caption end up close together in a shared vector space. At the end of each encoder, the whole input is averaged, or pooled, into one vector. A ten second clip becomes one vector, a caption becomes one vector, and the match between them is a single cosine similarity.
Pooling is efficient, and it throws information away. A ten second clip often holds several events at different moments: a door slams at second two, a dog barks at second five, rain continues underneath. Captions mirror this structure. "Dogs bark, then birds chirp" names two sources and two actions in order. Once the clip is squeezed into one vector, all of those events share a single point in space, and a caption that gets one of them wrong ("cats meow, then birds chirp") lands almost as close as the correct one.
Text search met the same problem years ago. ColBERT [3] introduced late interaction: keep one vector per token on both sides, and score a query against a document by letting every query token pick its most similar document token. This scoring rule, called MaxSim, made text retrieval more accurate and more robust, and the idea has since spread to images (ColPali [4]) and video (CLaMR [5]).
Audio has seen a few steps in this direction. ColQwen-Omni [22] is an open multi-vector retriever that can embed audio, but it was trained only on image and text pairs, so its audio search is zero-shot and aimed at spoken content such as podcasts and conversations. Wang, Gu and Ling [23] and Xin et al. [24] apply late interaction to AudioCaps and Clotho, matching audio frames against caption words with attention-based scoring, and neither releases code or model weights.
WavLate is an open late-interaction model trained for audio and caption retrieval. It keeps 32 vectors for every ten seconds of audio and one vector for every caption token, and scores pairs with plain MaxSim. Clips and captions are encoded independently, so every clip is indexed once and searched with any caption, and the index works with standard ColBERT search engines such as PLAID [18]. Where Wang, Gu and Ling use attention-based scoring and train on each benchmark's own data, WavLate pairs MaxSim with a training recipe built for multi-vector models. This post explains the architecture, the training recipe and the results against eight other open models, and releases everything needed to reproduce them.

Architecture

WavLate has two encoders and one scoring rule.
Audio tower. The audio is resampled to 32 kHz and cut into consecutive ten second windows, up to 30 seconds per clip. Each window becomes a log-mel spectrogram and passes through HTS-AT [6], initialised from MGA-CLAP [8]. HTS-AT processes the spectrogram with Swin Transformer [7] blocks and outputs 32 frame vectors per window, each covering about 0.31 seconds. We take MGA-CLAP's frame features before its pooling step, pass them through MGA-CLAP's frame projection (768 to 1024 dimensions) and a new linear layer down to 128 dimensions, and scale each vector to unit length. A 25 second clip therefore becomes 80 vectors: 32 for each full window and 16 for the final half window.
Text tower. Captions go through mLateOn [10]: a ModernBERT [9] encoder followed by ColBERT projection layers (768 to 1536 to 768 to 128 dimensions). Every token of the caption gets its own 128-dimensional unit vector. Special tokens and padding are masked out, so only the words of the caption take part in scoring.
Score. For a caption with token vectors q₁, …, qₙ and a clip with frame vectors d₁, …, dₘ, WavLate computes
score(q,d)=1n∑i=1nmax⁡j  qi⋅dj\text{score}(q, d) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \max_{j} \; q_i \cdot d_jscore(q,d)=n1​i=1∑n​jmax​qi​⋅dj​
Each caption token finds the moment of the clip it matches best, and the score averages those best matches. The figure above shows this for the caption "Dogs bark, Birds chirp": "Dogs" and "bark" match the first seconds, "Birds" and "chirp" match the later part, and the clip earns a high score because every word found its sound. The same score ranks clips for a caption (text to audio) and captions for a clip (audio to text).

Data

WavLate trains on 441,198 clips with 456,546 captions from three public datasets: WavCaps [11], AudioCaps [12] and Clotho [13]. The AudioCaps and Clotho test clips, and any WavCaps clips that overlap them, are removed. The table lists the 441,540 clips of the source manifest; 342 of them had no usable audio and were left out.

WavCaps captions were written by a language model from each clip's original metadata, while AudioCaps and Clotho captions were written by people.
Multinomial source sampling. Drawing clips uniformly would give WavCaps 88% of every batch and Clotho under 1%, so the model would rarely see human-written captions or long multi-event clips. WavLate builds each epoch with multinomial sampling over the three source datasets. Each source g with n_g clips receives a share of the epoch's draws proportional to n_g^α, with α = 0.5. An exponent of 1 reproduces the natural proportions and an exponent of 0 gives every source an equal share; 0.5 sits between the two and lifts the small, human-captioned sources. Two rules keep the repetition useful:

A clip is drawn at most as many times per epoch as it has captions (and at least twice), and each appearance pairs it with a different caption, so no clip and caption pair repeats within an epoch.
Draws that a capped source cannot use go to the remaining sources, so every epoch keeps 441,198 draws.

Loss

Each training step scores every caption in the batch against every clip in the batch with MaxSim. The loss has two parts.

Contrastive loss (multi-positive InfoNCE [14]). For each clip, its own captions should score higher than every other caption in the batch, and for each caption, its own clip should score higher than every other clip. A clip with several captions counts all of them as correct answers. The scores are divided by a learned temperature before the softmax, so the model also learns how sharp its rankings should be.
Distillation [15]. A frozen copy of pooled MGA-CLAP (the original single-vector model) also scores the batch. A KL divergence term, which measures how far one probability distribution is from another, pulls WavLate's ranking of the batch toward the teacher's ranking. The teacher supplies a graded sense of which wrong answers are nearly right, information that the contrastive loss alone does not carry.

Hard negatives

Random batches mostly contain easy negatives: a caption about rain is rarely confused with a clip of a guitar. WavLate learns more from close calls, so each clip gets 10 mined hard negatives, and batches are built so that a clip and its mined negatives train together.

MGA-CLAP embeds every clip and every caption.
For each clip, all training captions are ranked by similarity to the clip's audio. A candidate must score at least 0.01 below the clip's own best caption. The clip itself, other clips cut from the same YouTube video, and identical captions are skipped.
A mined negative can be a false negative: "a man speaks" fits thousands of clips, and training against such a caption would punish a correct match. Each candidate is therefore checked with a cross-encoder (cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-32m-v1, from the Ettin model suite [16]), a model that reads two captions together and scores how related they are. The threshold comes from the data itself. We measured how the cross-encoder scores two captions of the same clip and took the 0.9 quantile of those scores (9.94). A candidate whose captions reach that score reads like another description of the same clip, and is rejected.
The walk continues down the ranking until 10 candidates pass. Across the corpus, 6.5M candidates were checked and 32.2% were rejected.

Swap negatives. MaxSim scores a caption word by word, so it can learn to tell "a dog barks" from "a cat barks". Following CompA [25], which builds hard negative captions by swapping event order and attributes, about 45% of training captions get a swapped copy in which one sound word is replaced by an acoustically distinct word of the same kind (dog to cat, guitar to piano, rain to wind). Near-synonyms such as car and vehicle are never swapped. The swapped caption serves as an extra negative for its own clip only.

Training

Training runs for 5 epochs (4,310 steps). For the first 8% of steps both encoders are frozen and only the new audio projection and the temperature train, which keeps the randomly initialised projection from disturbing the pretrained encoders. Then everything trains together: encoder learning rates ramp up over 5% of the steps and follow a cosine decay to zero. The full run takes 7.4 hours on two A100 40 GB GPUs.
Contrastive learning improves with large batches, because each example meets more negatives. Multi-vector models make large batches expensive, since every clip carries dozens of vectors and every caption a dozen more. WavLate uses GradCache [17]. It first encodes the whole batch without storing activations, computes the loss and the gradient of the loss with respect to every embedding, then encodes the batch again in small chunks and backpropagates those stored gradients through the encoders.

One general model. Every model we ran is evaluated as released, with no fine-tuning on AudioCaps or Clotho alone. The AudioCaps and Clotho training splits are part of the training data of every model listed, including WavLate.

Among the open models, WavLate has the best mean Recall@1 (37.9) and Recall@10 (79.4) and the best score on every Clotho metric, by 3.1 to 6.0 points over the next best single-vector model (3.8 and 3.1 points at Recall@1). Clotho clips run 15 to 30 seconds and their captions describe several events, which is the setting where matching words to moments should help most. On AudioCaps, WavLate leads text to audio Recall@1 (43.6) among the open models, and M2D-CLAP leads audio to text Recall@1 (58.6 against 53.6). WavLate improves on MGA-CLAP, the model whose audio encoder it starts from, by 2.0 points of mean Recall@1, with training data from the same sources.
To check that this gap is larger than the noise of a test set with about a thousand clips, we ran a paired bootstrap. A bootstrap redraws the test clips at random with replacement, together with their captions, 10,000 times and recomputes both models' scores on each redraw; "paired" means both models are scored on the same redraws. The 95% interval for WavLate's lead over MGA-CLAP in mean Recall@1 is 0.8 to 3.2 points, and MGA-CLAP came out ahead in 0.09% of the redraws. Every Clotho metric and AudioCaps text to audio Recall@1 show a clear lead. AudioCaps audio to text Recall@1 is a statistical tie (WavLate 1.0 points lower, interval −4.5 to +2.2).
The two WavLate variants at the top of the table are described in the next section. The last row copies the numbers reported for Multiscale Matching [23], a late-interaction setup without released weights, measured on a 957-clip AudioCaps test set.

Other base models and teachers

WavLate depends on two pretrained CLAP models: one supplies the starting weights of the audio encoder (the base model), and a frozen pooled copy of one acts as the teacher, which mines the hard negatives and provides the distillation targets. The released WavLate uses MGA-CLAP for both roles. We trained two more versions with the same data, recipe and 5 epochs to see how much each role matters.

A different teacher. Keeping MGA-CLAP's audio encoder and switching the teacher to M2D-CLAP 2025 [19] raises mean Recall@1 from 37.9 to 38.6, with the largest change on AudioCaps (audio to text 53.6 to 56.2, text to audio 43.6 to 44.9). M2D-CLAP's similarity scores spread over a narrower range than MGA-CLAP's: on the same 4,000 training clips the gap between matching and non-matching pairs is 0.16 in cosine similarity against 0.31, while both teachers rank the right caption first equally often (34%). We therefore scaled the M2D-CLAP teacher's scores by 40 instead of 20 before the distillation softmax, so both teachers give targets of the same sharpness.
A different base model. WavLate-M2D replaces the audio encoder as well. M2D-CLAP's audio encoder is a Vision Transformer (ViT, a Transformer that reads the spectrogram as a grid of 16 by 16 patches) that takes 16 kHz audio in windows of 10 seconds. For each window we average its patch outputs over frequency to get one vector per time step and then average neighbouring pairs, which gives 31 vectors of about 0.32 seconds, the same granularity as the HTS-AT version. M2D-CLAP's own pooling head is dropped, and a new linear layer maps the 768-dimensional frames to 128 dimensions. Nothing else changes: the text tower, the MaxSim score, the loss, the swap negatives and the sampling stay as described above, with M2D-CLAP mining the hard negatives.
WavLate-M2D gains 5.5 points of mean Recall@1 over pooled M2D-CLAP, the model it starts from, and leads every Recall@1 column of the results table: 62.9 and 49.6 on AudioCaps, 30.7 and 24.5 on Clotho. The gain over the base model is larger here than for MGA-CLAP (5.5 against 2.0 points), so the recipe carries over to a second, architecturally different audio encoder.
WavLate-M2D's weights are not released. M2D and M2D-CLAP are distributed under NTT's evaluation license, which allows research evaluation and forbids redistributing modified weights.

WavLate-M2D uses the same settings except for the audio side: M2D-CLAP 2025 initialisation, 16 kHz mono input, 10 s windows with 31 frames each (768 dimensions before the 128-dimensional projection), M2D-CLAP as miner and teacher, and teacher scores scaled by 40.

Using WavLate

WavLate loads with transformers through AutoModel.
import soundfile as sf
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("chungimungi/WavLate", trust_remote_code=True).eval()

captions = ["A dog barks while birds chirp", "Rain falls on a tin roof"]
wave, rate = sf.read("clip.wav", dtype="float32")
if wave.ndim > 1:
wave = wave.mean(axis=1) # mix down to mono

with torch.inference_mode():
text, text_mask = model.encode_text(captions)
audio, audio_mask = model.encode_audio([wave], sampling_rate=rate)
scores = model.score(text, text_mask, audio, audio_mask) # [captions, clips]
print(scores)

The released model reproduces the numbers in this post. Its vectors match the training code exactly, and both test pools were rerun from the released checkpoint.
The dataset repository holds the training records with their hard negatives, all of the training audio (32 kHz FLAC in tar shards, each row records its shard and byte offset), and the two test pools with audio:
from datasets import load_dataset

train = load_dataset("chungimungi/WavLate-training-data", "training", split="train")
clotho = load_dataset("chungimungi/WavLate-training-data", "evaluation", split="clotho_evaluation")
